title: How we built Lead Zeppelin with Unity and Codex — architecture, generated art, boss systems, and testing
author: No-Communication7253
selftext:
Lead Zeppelin started with a pretty straightforward idea: a *Heavy Weapon*\-inspired scrolling shooter where you pilot a heavily armed zeppelin, with an industrial aesthetic and a rock soundtrack.

The development process has been iterative. I provide the concept, creative direction, mechanic requests, and feedback from playing the builds. Codex handles programming and development tooling. We build something playable, identify specific problems, and revise it.

Here’s the technical breakdown:

***The foundation is Unity 6 and C#.***

The project uses Unity **6000.3.25f1**, the **Universal Render Pipeline’s 2D renderer**, Unity’s **Input System**, and **uGUI/TextMeshPro**. Gameplay uses an orthographic camera with a consistent 16:9 playfield. Scrolling backgrounds, foreground layers, enemies, projectiles, and effects create the movement through each environment.

***One bootstrap scene assembles the game at runtime.***

The main `Sortie` component coordinates the game’s states: overworld, hangar, combat, pause, defeat, and completion. Responsibilities are divided between several systems:Larger systems are split across C# partial-class files by feature or encounter. Moving between flights updates the active encounter and scenery while carrying hull, weapons, score, and cooldowns forward.

***Combat runs through a shared update loop.***

Enemies and shots are tracked in collections and advanced by the combat manager. Sprite renderers are pooled and reused for gameplay objects and effects. Projectile collisions use swept checks between the projectile’s previous and current positions against elliptical hit regions. That addresses fast shots crossing a target between frames. There are also separate rules for weak points, destructible ordnance, guided missiles, deflected projectiles, and environmental forces.

***Bosses combine reusable attacks with individual mechanics.***

The established boss structure gives each boss three attacks associated with its destination and three signature attacks. Their rotation alternates between those groups and retains its position across health phases. Difficulty has separate controls for projectile speed, attack frequency, health, and additional Boss Rush abilities.

For example, campaign projectile speed follows:`1.15 × 1.10^(destination − 1)`

Boss attack frequency increases by 10 percentage points for each completed 10% of health lost. Warning durations are controlled separately, which lets us increase pressure while preserving reaction cues.Persistent attacks also need scheduling rules. A wind field or deployed battery can remain active long after its initial launch, so checking only the next attack’s cooldown can create excessive overlap.

***Generated artwork becomes a collection of working mechanical parts.***

Image generation supplies illustrated assets, but integrating them requires additional work. A Python pipeline uses Pillow and NumPy to extract moving components from painted sprites and export a JSON rig catalog. Unity reads measurements for pivots, dimensions, rotation limits, and attachment positions. That supports aiming cannons, recoil, spinning propellers, and animated fans. Some assets needed revised artwork to remove a painted barrel from the stationary hull before attaching the moving version. Custom shaders animate selected regions for plasma, lightning, steam, pressure waves, and fan apertures. This lets the metal housing stay still while its internal machinery moves.

***Progression and input are shared across several modes.***

Campaign progress is stored as versioned JSON through Unity’s `PlayerPrefs`, including salvage, upgrades, stage unlocks, and Boss Rush records. Campaign runs, individual practice flights, and Boss Rush share combat systems but apply different progression rules. Practice can use either stock equipment or purchased upgrades. Menus support mouse, keyboard, D-pad, and stick navigation. They also handle focus restoration, held-input repeat, device-specific prompts, and returning a held stick to neutral after changing menus. Those details needed explicit testing to prevent double purchases and accidental activation.

***Audio has its own preparation and playback pipeline.***

Early music was synthesized with Python, NumPy, and SciPy. The later soundtrack uses Suno tracks prepared as full-length masters with consistent loudness and peak targets, then streamed through Unity as Vorbis. The radio uses two music sources for crossfading and a separate effects source. Area playlists continue across stage boundaries and boss entrances, with **3.5-second song crossfades**. Playlist length uses the scripted approach durations; the closing song repeats to accommodate variable boss-fight lengths.

***Verification includes compiled-player diagnostics and human playtesting.***

We use scripted Unity builds, isolated QA save profiles, runtime assertions, screenshots, and targeted diagnostic players. One concrete example was Storm Regent’s overlapping wind patterns. In a repeatable 60-second diagnostic at 10% boss health, overlapping major fields dropped from **55.92 seconds to zero** after adding scheduling guards.That establishes that the scheduling fix worked. Judging whether the fight feels fair still requires playing it. Windows builds are automated through editor scripts. The demo uses a compile-time flag, separate save storage, restricted campaign access, and ZIP packaging.

The recurring work has been turning each idea into specific behavior, then checking how it interacts with everything already present: attack timing, sprite alignment, collision regions, controller focus, save compatibility, audio transitions, and the final executable.

Check out the demo on itch: [https://idi-studios-inc.itch.io/lead-zeppelin-demo](https://idi-studios-inc.itch.io/lead-zeppelin-demo)
